title: The UAE Is Secretly Helping Ansarallah Fight Saudi Arabia in Yemen
author: Ryan Grim

media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F15011025-5981-4c77-a134-e2343c2d8fa7_4200x2800.jpeg)A
fighter loyal to Yemen's Saud-backed internationally-recognized government
fires a turret from the back of a pickup truck at a position along the
frontlines against Ansarallah around Mount al-Midan in Yemen's western Taiz
province on October 26, 2026. Photo by Ahmad AL-BASHA / AFP via Getty Images.

The United Arab Emirates, a key American and Israeli ally in the Gulf, has
been quietly assisting Ansarallah in its conflict against Saudi-backed forces
inside Yemen, four sources with knowledge of the situation told Drop Site
News.

Specifically, various UAE-aligned Yemeni forces have been providing targeting
assistance to Ansarallah in their battle against Saudi-backed government
forces in Yemen while Abu Dhabi has looked the other way, the sources said.

According to two sources with knowledge of the covert arrangement, the UAE's
assistance has also included direct sharing of intelligence by the UAE itself
to Ansarallah for the purpose of targeting Saudi-backed forces.

A Yemeni source familiar with the Ansarallah backchannel confirmed that "the
UAE has passed a significant amount of intelligence to the Sana'a-based
government; the line of communication between the two sides remains open." The
Yemeni source told Drop Site that Ansarallah "established their own channels
of communication internally with military commanders" who remain loyal to the
UAE. The sources required anonymity as they are not authorized to speak
publicly about the arrangement.

That the UAE is directly aiding one of its chief regional opponents is
extraordinary. The UAE and Ansarallah are fierce ideological enemies with
geopolitical goals that are in direct opposition to one another. The UAE is a
close ally of Israel and the United States while Ansarallah is a close ally of
Iran. However, when it comes to Yemen, their interests have come to overlap to
some extent, producing a classic enemy-of-my enemy situation. The UAE was
sidelined in Yemen earlier this year by Saudi Arabia, and stands to regain a
strategic foothold in Yemen in the current conflict.

The assistance to Ansarallah from the UAE, some of the sources said, does not
include help with intelligence and targeting inside Saudi Arabia, but is
limited to help with targeting and intelligence inside Yemen. Ansarallah's
attacks on Saudi Arabia included strikes on Saudi's main airport, one of which
killed 12 people and wounded more than 300 others--and led to the cancellation
of the Future Investment Initiative conference, otherwise known as the "Davos
in the Desert."

Recently, according to one source, a senior American official warned the
Emirates that the U.S. had learned of the covert assistance being provided and
urged that it be ended. Sources indicated the intelligence assistance was
ongoing. UAE Ambassador to the U.S. Yousef Al Otaiba did not respond to
requests for comment.

Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a senior Ansarallah official, denied that the UAE was
assisting Ansarallah but insisted the Emirates were committed to neutrality.
"The UAE has not provided any form of support to Yemen--neither against Saudi
Arabia nor against its proxies within Yemen," he told Drop Site. "According to
our information, the UAE remains committed to neutrality and has refused to
become re-involved in the aggression against Yemen alongside Saudi Arabia,
despite persistent efforts by [Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed] bin Salman to
persuade it to join."

Last month, the Iran-backed Ansarallah, also known as the Houthis, launched a
blitz to the Red Sea coast that stunned the region, routed Saudi-backed
forces, and left Ansarallah in control of the Bab Al-Mandab Strait, one of the
world's busiest shipping lanes and an important alternative to the blockaded
Strait of Hormuz. Saudi efforts to regain territory have largely been
repelled. Since then, Saudi Arabia has increasingly bombed Sana'a and other
Ansarallah-controlled areas, while Ansarallah have conducted multiple strikes
on Saudi Arabia.

Beginning in 2015, the Emirates were allied with Saudi Arabia as part of a
coalition backing the Yemeni government, after Ansarallah swept south from its
stronghold in the northern highlands and took over Sana'a in 2014. The Yemeni
government is commonly referred to as the internationally recognized
government, or IRG, and it remains largely based in Riyadh. But, early in the
conflict, the UAE's aims and ambitions were at odds with the Saudis, causing
division in the anti-Ansarallah side. In December of last year, that friction
resulted in clashes between UAE-backed forces and Saudi-backed military units
in the south and the UAE was effectively
[expelled](https://www.dropsitenews.com/p/yemen-uae-saudi-southern-
transitional-council) from Yemen by force.

Earlier this month, [The Guardian
reported](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/17/uae-yemen-conflict-
agreement-saudi-arabia-houthi-gains) that the UAE was re-entering the Yemeni
conflict on the side of Saudi Arabia by agreeing to resume some payments to
some of the forces it had backed.

That backing would most likely come through supporting the Giants "Al
Amaliqah" Brigades, a predominantly Salafi militia ideologically opposed to
the Houthis with an estimated 20,000 to 30,000 largely southern fighters. The
Southern Giants are[ currently
battling](https://alamalika.net/site/2026/10/23/%D9%82%D9%88%D8%A7%D8%AA-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B9%D9%85%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%82%D8%A9-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AC%D9%86%D9%88%D8%A8%D9%8A%D8%A9-%D8%AA%D9%83%D8%B3%D8%B1-%D9%87%D8%AC%D9%88%D9%85-%D8%AD%D9%88%D8%AB%D9%8A/)
for control of the Kahboub mountain range overlooking the Bab al-Mandab.

This potential support has not been reflected on the battlefield, the Yemeni
source said. Many commanders within the Giants Brigades have deceived the
Saudi-backed forces, the source said, repeatedly abandoning their positions
without any engagement or confrontation.

The source also told Drop Site that military unit commanders affiliated with
the UAE-backed Southern Transitional Council (STC) have refrained from
fighting the Houthis, effectively stalling battlefronts--particularly in the
southern governorates of Al-Dhale, and Lahj--bordering Taiz governorate, and
frequently withdraw from their positions.

A UAE-based senior official categorically stated to Drop Site that "the STC
has no channels of communication with the Houthis" and denied that STC were
refusing to fight Ansarallah in the south.**** "The STC has publicly and
consistently maintained that the Southern Armed Forces will not participate in
military operations in the North," Amr al-Beidh, special representative of the
president of the STC, told Drop Site. "This should not be confused with an
unwillingness to confront the Houthis. Quite the opposite. Any Houthi advance
towards the South will be met with resistance."

"It is important to distinguish between our policy of not engaging in military
operations in the north and our firm commitment to defending the South against
the Houthis," he added.

The White House and a spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition did not respond
to requests for comment.

More than 250,000 people have been displaced by the escalating violence since
August 1, [according to](https://dtm.iom.int/reports/yemen-displacement-
caused-escalation-western-yemen-update-15-21-october-2026?close=true) the
International Organization for Migration. Almost half of those have fled Taiz
governorate, which encompasses some of Yemen's highest mountains and a large
stretch of the western Red Sea coastal plain approaching the Bab al-Mandab,
including the strategic port of Mokha. Aid agencies cannot reach more than
600,000 people in Taiz--where the capital city is currently besieged by
Ansarallah--who depend on humanitarian assistance, according to the UN's World
Food Program (WFP), including more than 200,000 women and children.

[READ MORE: Encircled by War, Yemen's Taiz Residents Brace for Fighting and a
Renewed Siege](https://www.dropsitenews.com/p/yemen-taiz-ansarallah-siege-
fuel-food-crisis)

## **A Web of War**

The UAE is Israel's closest ally in the Gulf, and was previously allied with
Saudi Arabia in its war against Ansarallah in Yemen. But the UAE's interests
in Yemen diverge from both Israel's and Saudi Arabia's.

As early as 2015 it became apparent that the Emirates' priority in Yemen was
to counter the perceived threat from the Muslim Brotherhood over and above the
conflict with Ansarallah. The Islah Party--Yemen's political Islamist party
that includes factions of the Muslim Brotherhood--emerged as the UAE's primary
target despite their role within the IRG.

In 2015, UAE forces and Yemeni fighters it trained and funded pushed Houthi
forces--that at the time included loyalists of Yemen's former president Ali
Abdullah Saleh--out of the southern city of Aden. The UAE went on to
consolidate its gains, establishing an array of fighting groups that they both
funded and directed.

The STC represented the aspiration for renewed southern independence and
animosity in the region toward being ruled by northern elites since the
unification of Yemen in 1990. Unification resulted in land theft and the
economic benefits of the south's natural resources being captured by Saleh and
his cronies. Islah was also viewed by southerners as part of this exploitative
northern rule.

The UAE capitalized on this animosity and desire for self-determination,
supporting the creation in May 2017 of the separatist Southern Transitional
Council (STC) led by Aidarous al-Zubaidi. Islah was a common enemy.

Between 2015 and 2018 at least 160 assassinations were carried out in southern
Yemen. The majority of those assassinated were members of Islah, many of them
were imams, creating a climate of fear and paranoia in Aden and across the
south. Widely held suspicion that the UAE was behind the deaths was confirmed
in 2018 when American mercenaries told a[
BuzzFeed](https://www.buzzfeednews.com/article/aramroston/mercenaries-
assassination-us-yemen-uae-spear-golan-dahlan) journalist (and, later,[ the
BBC](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Z51MTI9sbFY)) that they had carried out
assassinations on behalf of the UAE and trained Yemeni forces to carry on the
killings.

Ansaf Ali Mayo, an Islah parliamentarian, survived an attempt on his life by
the American assassins. Earlier this year he[ filed a
lawsuit](https://cja.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/03/001.Complaint.2025.12.23.pdf) against the two former
U.S. special forces operators in a federal court in San Diego along with the
Israeli-Hungarian founder of the private security firm Spear Operations Group
that hired them.

The UAE's hiring of foreign mercenaries didn't stop at U.S. veterans.
Thousands of Sudanese Rapid Support Force (RSF) were brought in by the UAE
between 2015 and 2018 to help fight Ansarallah as the UAE-backed forces made
gains up Yemen's western Red Sea coast into the governorate of Hodeidah, home
to Yemen's second largest port and controlled by Ansarallah.

The rift between UAE-backed forces and those of the Saudi-backed IRG has not
only considerably weakened efforts against the Houthis but, on several
occasions over the past decade, spilled into direct infighting.

In August 2019, UAE fighter jets carried out up to 24 airstrikes [against
IRG](https://mailchi.mp/7c6cd4284d06/september2019-yemen-data-project-
update-563155?e=\[UNIQID\]) and Islah-aligned government military units and
positions in Aden, Abyan, and Marib[ in support of the
STC](https://web.archive.org/web/20190923112017/https:/uk.reuters.com/article/uk-
yemen-security-explainer/explainer-saudi-arabia-struggles-to-hold-yemen-
coalition-together-as-allies-face-off-idUKKCN1VN0YD) as the competing
factions[ vied for
control](https://web.archive.org/web/20190915090349/https:/www.gulf-
times.com/story/640361/UAE-air-raids-raise-tensions-with-Yemen-govt). Al-
Zubaidi was summoned to the Saudi capital and in November 2019, an agreement
was signed between the Saudi-backed IRG and the STC.

The power-sharing deal, known as the Riyadh Agreement, should have meant an
integration of STC forces into the IRG military in exchange for southern
representation in a unity government. But implementation stalled.

The situation came to a head in December 2025 when STC forces swept east from
their stronghold in Aden to take two large governorates bordering Saudi Arabia
and Oman. Saudi Arabia responded by launching airstrikes targeting a large
shipment of Emirati military equipment at the port of Mukalla and giving the
UAE 24 hours to leave and end its "military or financial support to any party
within Yemen." The UAE heeded the warnings and STC forces were quickly routed
by Yemeni government military units backed by Saudi air cover.

"Saudi Arabia was the one that forced the UAE out of the coalition waging war
on Yemen in a humiliating manner, effectively shooting itself in the foot,"
said al-Bukhaiti. "Given this experience, it is only natural that the UAE
would refuse to rejoin the Saudi-led coalition in its aggression against Yemen
[Ansarallah], despite pressure from Saudi Arabia, the United States, and
Israel, particularly after Yemen demonstrated its remarkable ability to defend
itself and impose a principle of blockade for blockade and escalation for
escalation."

Since this latest fissure between Saudi Arabia and the UAE in Yemen, not all
of the formerly UAE-aligned forces have been fully integrated into the IRG
military and security apparatus, partially because this process was disrupted
due to the renewed fighting with Ansarallah. STC loyalists remain in the
mountains of Al Dhale, the homeland of Al-Zubaidi who fled to the UAE in
January. For months after the Saudi pushback in December 2025, surveillance
drones were a constant presence and Saudi airstrikes killed at least six
civilians in Al Dhale in January. A Yemeni source familiar with the STC-
Ansarallah communications told Drop Site that channels were being facilitated
by a senior STC figure in Al-Dhale.

In an indication of both how the UAE operates in Yemen and sentiment in the
south towards the Saudi-backed IRG, when asked by Drop Site which of the
fighting groups formerly funded and commanded by the UAE would likely provide
intelligence to the Houthis for targeting IRG forces, an individual close to
the STC quipped, "probably all of them."

Ansarallah, in recent months, has been remarkably effective at targeting
commanders among the Saudi-backed fighters and in anticipating the movements
of their forces. Two rounds of precision strikes on October 2 and 7 at the
coalition military base west of Aden put this on display. One hit the doorway
to the office of the Saudi commander, though he was not present. Another hit
brand new military vehicles that were brought to the base a few hours earlier.

The UAE has advanced intelligence gathering capabilities. Established in 2009,
the UAE's cybersurveillance Project Raven surveilled alleged militants while
also monitoring foreign governments _,_ human rights activists and those
critical of the Emirati monarchy. Former U.S. intelligence operatives
including former NSA employees were heavily involved in aiding and training
the Emiratis, according to an investigation[ by
Reuters.](https://www.reuters.com/investigates/special-report/usa-spying-
raven/) By 2013, Reuters reported, the majority of Raven's workforce were
Americans. Beginning in 2016, the team used the spying platform Karam to hack
into the iPhones of foreign leaders including Turkey's Defense Minister, the
Emir of Qatar and Yemeni Nobel Prize-winning political activist Tawakkol
Karman.

The UAE is also known to have deployed sophisticated Israeli spyware. In 2021
Amnesty's Pegasus Project investigation determined that the UAE had begun
using NSO Group's Pegasus spyware to target members of the Saudi-backed
internationally recognized government for surveillance.

Bukhaiti said that the alignment of interests does not mean there is an
official alliance between Ansarallah and the UAE. "However, this does not mean
that an alliance exists between the UAE and Yemen out of spite toward Saudi
Arabia or as a means of settling scores with it. As for reports circulating
about an attempt by the UAE to contact us to form an alliance against Saudi
Arabia, they are entirely baseless," he said. "Saudi Arabia does not need to
beg countries around the world to defend it, nor does it need to worry about
the possibility of a future Yemeni-Emirati alliance against it. All it needs
to do is agree to end the war and lift the blockade on both sides. This is the
only genuine way out of this conflict."

Al-Bukhaiti's reference to "the possibility of a future Yemeni-Emirati
alliance" contains a thinly veiled suggestion: Saudi Arabia, he said, need not
worry about such an alliance, as long as they end the war and lift the
blockade. If they do not do so, however, the potential of such an alliance
hangs over the conflict.
